question: Is EUR 17 billion for a battery-based electricity storage scheme optimal use of EU taxpayers’ money?

As part of the European Green Deal and ‘Fit for 55’ objectives the Commission has recently approved an EUR 17.7 billion EU-funded centralised electricity storage system in Italy. The system is primarily battery-based and will have a capacity of over 71 GWh.1 However, considering the massive investment and technology developments in the energy field, the cost-effectiveness and strategic impact of this project warrant thorough scrutiny. 1.

As the storage system’s capacity represents only 0.022 % of Italy’s annual energy consumption, can the Commission outline how this aligns with effective energy integration and grid stability, particularly when alternative strategies, such as scaling up energy production, would offer more substantial benefits?

How does the Commission justify this financial commitment to battery-based storage technology, especially when considering the limitations in storage duration and capacity and the impact on the ongoing lithium shortage.
Has the Commission carried out an independent impact assessment of this scheme?
answer: EN E-000053/24 on behalf of the Commission (13.2.2024) On 22 December 2023, the Commission authorised, under EU State aid rules, notably in the light of the Guidelines on State aid for climate, environmental protection and energy 20221 an Italian measure supporting the development of electricity storage.

In its decision2, the Commission has found that the planned Italian scheme is consistent with the EU’s 2030 climate target and 2050 climate neutrality target. While the scheme contributes to the objectives of the European Green Deal, it is important to understand that the approval under EU State aid rules only concerns the compatibility of the Italian measure with the European State aid rules.

State aid approval does not result in the provision of money from the EU budget. The measure at issue is proposed by Italy and assessed for compliance with State aid requirements by the Commission. Developing storage, including battery storage has been recognized in recent EU policy actions as an important contribution to the energy transition3.

The Italian authorities have analysed certain scenarios of the future Italian electricity system and found a need for more flexibility such as electricity storage including batteries and pumped hydro storage facilities. In their submission, the Italian authorities described the expected main source of funding to be the revenues from tenders for using the storage capacity on the relevant electricity markets.

Remaining contributions will be made by the Italian producers and consumers (balancing responsible parties) via a levy. In this respect, it should be noted that the scheme will be open to all electricity storage technologies fulfilling the criteria of technical and commercial readiness as defined by the Italian authorities.
